content_html:
Gross margin and markup both describe the profit you make on a sale, but they measure it against different numbers. Margin compares profit with the selling price; markup compares it with the cost. Mixing them up is one of the most common pricing mistakes in small businesses. This calculator works out the cost, selling price, profit, margin and markup from any two values you know, and shows the price you would need to charge for a range of target margins.

How to use this calculator

  1. I know the: choose the pair of values you already have, such as your cost and the margin you want, or the price a competitor charges and the markup you normally use.
  2. Enter the two values. Costs and prices are per unit. Margins and markups are percentages.
  3. Units sold (optional): enter a quantity to see total revenue, cost and gross profit for an order or a month of sales.

Margin and markup formulas

  • Gross profit = selling price − cost
  • Gross margin = gross profit ÷ selling price
  • Markup = gross profit ÷ cost
  • Price from a target margin = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
  • Price from a markup = cost × (1 + markup)

To convert between the two: markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin), and margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup). Because the selling price is always larger than the cost when you make a profit, the margin percentage is always smaller than the markup percentage for the same sale.

A worked example

An item costs you $60 and sells for $100. The gross profit is $40. Divided by the $100 price, that is a 40% gross margin; divided by the $60 cost, it is a 66.67% markup. Sell 250 of them and you take in $25,000 of revenue on $15,000 of cost, a gross profit of $10,000.

Now suppose you want a 40% margin on a different item that costs $60 but you add only a 40% markup. The price becomes $84 and the margin drops to 28.57%, far short of the goal. Pricing with the target margin formula, $60 ÷ (1 − 0.40), gives the correct $100.

Pricing tips

  • Include every direct cost in the unit cost: purchase price, freight in, packaging and payment processing if it varies with each sale.
  • Gross margin has to cover rent, wages, marketing and other overheads before any net profit is left, so a healthy-looking margin can still mean a loss overall.
  • Discounts eat into margin faster than you might expect: a 20% discount on an item with a 40% margin cuts the margin to 25%.
  • When you talk with suppliers, buyers or accountants, say whether a percentage is a margin or a markup to avoid confusion.

faq.question: Is margin or markup better for pricing?
faq.answer: Neither is better; they describe the same profit differently. Many retailers set prices with a markup on cost because it is quick to apply, while financial statements and lenders usually look at margin. What matters is knowing which one a figure refers to.

faq.question: Can markup be more than 100%?
faq.answer: Yes. A 100% markup means the price is double the cost, and markups of several hundred percent are common for low-cost items. Gross margin, on the other hand, can never reach 100% unless the item costs nothing.

faq.question: What is the difference between gross margin and net margin?
faq.answer: Gross margin subtracts only the direct cost of the goods sold. Net margin subtracts every expense, including rent, wages, marketing, interest and taxes, so it is always lower than gross margin.

faq.question: What happens if the selling price is lower than the cost?
faq.answer: The profit is negative, so the calculator shows a negative margin and markup. That means each sale loses money before overheads are even counted.

faq.question: Is this the same as a stock margin calculator?
faq.answer: No. This tool is for profit margin and markup on products and services. Buying stocks on margin means borrowing from a broker, which is a different calculation.
